title: Infra: GPU Fleet, Capacity & IaC Strategy (playbook)
author: Asha Patel
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook documents Redwood Inference's canonical approach for GPU fleet capacity planning, cloud account and networking boundaries, Terraform / IaC module layout, CI/CD and build pipelines, and operational runbooks for day-2 activities. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners who operate the inference-serving fleet.

Scope
-----
- GPU fleet sizing and tier definitions (hosted + dedicated pools)
- Cloud account structure and network topology for regions and tenants
- Terraform module standards, state management, and CI/CD practices
- Runbooks for scaling, incident triage, and failure recovery
- Cross-team ownership and handoffs (capacity, oncall, cost)

Ownership
---------
- Capacity forecasting & quotas: infra-scheduling (team)
- Terraform modules & CI pipelines: infra-iac (team)
- VPC, peering, and network security: infra-networking (team)
- Oncall & incident runbooks: eng-sre (team)
- Cost monitoring and alerts: finance + infra (shared)

GPU Fleet & Capacity Model
-------------------------
Goals: keep 99th-percentile tail latency below SLOs while minimizing idle GPUs and cost. Model supports three capacity tiers:

1) On-demand (burst)
   - Purpose: absorb short-lived load spikes, dev/test bursts
   - Backing infra: cloud ephemeral instances (preemptible where acceptable)
   - Target utilization: 5-25% (buffer for spikes)

2) Reserved (steady)
   - Purpose: predictable throughput for production hosted API
   - Backing infra: Dedicated GPU pools / reserved instances
   - Target utilization: 55-80%

3) High-availability (HA) pools
   - Purpose: reserved for SLA-backed Dedicated customers and control-plane critical workloads
   - Backing infra: zonal/regionally distributed, reserved capacity
   - Target utilization: 40-70% (lower to maintain headroom for failover)

Capacity thresholds and SLOs
- Fleet headroom target: maintain 15% spare GPUs in Reserved tier for the next 24h forecast window.
- Autoscaling baseline: when mean queued requests per GPU > 0.8 for 5m and 90th latency > 80% of SLO, trigger scale-up.
- Scale down guardrails: only if 24h predicted utilization falls below 60% and 95th latency < 50% of SLO for 2h.

Forecasting inputs (daily run)
- 7/14/30-day traffic windows (weighted)
- Model mix (seq length distribution, model variants, batching efficiency)
- Known reserved commitments and scheduled rollouts
- Hardware performance profiles (tokens/sec per GPU by model)

Example capacity calculation (text)
- Expected peak tokens/sec = 600k
- Model throughput per GPU = 6k tokens/sec -> Needed GPUs = ceil(600k / 6k) = 100 GPUs -> add 15% headroom -> 115 GPUs

Scaling runbook (operational)
----------------------------
1) Situation: 95th latency > SLO or queue backlog increasing rapidly
2) Triage steps:
   - Check dashboards: per-pool queued requests, mean batch size, kernel errors
   - Identify impacted pool(s) and region(s)
   - Verify autoscaler logs: whether scale actions are pending/failed
3) If autoscaler failed to add capacity:
   - Run terraform job to increase desired count for pool (see Terraform section)
   - If CI/CD blocked, follow CI pipeline troubleshooting steps below
4) If all pools are saturated and we need fast temporary capacity:
   - Trigger on-demand burst pool via console / infra-runbook CLI (prevalidated image)
   - Apply traffic routing policy (smart routing) to send non-critical requests to slower or quantized model variants
5) Post-incident actions:
   - Annotate incident ticket with root cause and action taken
   - Update forecasts and increase baseline pool if warranted

Terraform / IaC module standards
-------------------------------
Principles:
- Small, composable modules (networking, instance-pool, autoscaler, iam, monitoring)
- Clear separation between env-specific overlay (dev/staging/prod) and reusable modules
- Idempotent modules with safe defaults and explicit opt-ins for destructive configs
- Strong input/output typing and documentation in module README

Module layout (recommended)
- modules/networking/  -> vpc, subnets, peering, route-tables
- modules/gpu-pool/    -> instance groups, instance templates, startup scripts, taints/labels
- modules/autoscaler/  -> HPA/cluster-autoscaler config, scale policies, cooldowns
- modules/iam/         -> roles, policies scoped to least privilege
- modules/monitoring/  -> metrics, dashboards, alerts, log sinks

Naming conventions
- Resource IDs: rwinf-{env}-{region}-{component}-{short-id}
- Terraform workspaces: rwinf-{env}-{region} (e.g., rwinf-prod-us-west1)

State management and locking
- Remote backend: hosted state (S3/GCS) with server-side encryption and strict ACLs
- Locking: DynamoDB or Cloud Storage lock object to prevent concurrent apply collisions
- State access: restricted to CI service principal + infra-admin role via IAM

Example terraform snippet (module usage)
```
module "gpu_pool_west" {
  source = "git::ssh://git.example.com/infra/modules/gpu-pool.git//modules/gke"
  env    = "prod"
  region = "us-west1"
  instance_type = "a100-40gb"
  desired_count  = 50
  min_count = 10
  max_count = 200
  labels = { pool = "reserved" }
}
```

CI/CD and build pipelines
------------------------
Goals: safe automated changes to infra with strong reviews, automated plan outputs, gated applies, and environment promotion flow.

Pipeline stages (canonical):
1) lint + validate (tf fmt, tf validate, module unit tests)
2) plan (create plan artifact, upload to PR comment)
3) manual review & approvals (required for prod changes)
4) apply (runs with service principal and state lock)
5) post-apply smoke tests (create test VM/ping service, validate metrics)

Policies:
- No direct commits to main for production-affecting modules; use PRs with at least two approvers.
- Applies to prod require a release approver with infra-admin role.
- Plan artifacts must be stored and linked to the change ticket for audit.

Secrets and service principals
- CI uses ephemeral short-lived credentials where supported (workload identity, oauth).
- Terraform provider credentials are stored in secret manager with strict ACLs and rotated quarterly.

Cloud accounts & networking (recommended topology)
------------------------------------------------
High-level account strategy:
- Management account: centralized billing, shared services, org-level policies
- Prod account(s): one per cloud region or major customer cohort for Dedicated customers as needed
- Non-prod accounts: dev, staging, perf-bench (isolated)

Network topology:
- VPC per account with standard CIDR allocations (documented centrally)
- Hub-and-spoke model for shared services (logging, monitoring, artifact registry)
- Inter-region VPC peering or Transit Gateway for cross-region failover (encrypted)

Security & IAM patterns
- Use least-privilege IAM roles for instance pools and CI service accounts
- GPU node pools run under a constrained node IAM role with no ability to modify infra state
- Control-plane operations use a separate admin role with MFA enforced

Day-2 operations and runbooks
---------------------------
Runbook: Add capacity to pool (quick)
1) Open runbook ticket and notify oncall channel (#infra-oncall)
2) Confirm forecast and need (check forecasting job outputs)
3) Create PR to overlay workspace to increment desired_count for pool (dev/staging first if unsure)
4) Trigger pipeline, review plan, apply to targeted workspace
5) Validate by checking pool desired vs actual, and run post-apply smoke tests
6) Close ticket and update capacity model

Runbook: Recover from network partition affecting GPU pool
1) Identify affected subnets and endpoints via monitoring dashboards
2) Reconcile route tables and firewall rules in network module outputs
3) If peering broken, follow 'repair peering' documented steps (link to module README)
4) If instances are unhealthy, use instance replacement job (automated) or run manual node drain and recreate
5) Post-incident: run network connectivity tests across zones and publish findings

Observability and telemetry
-------------------------
Essential metrics to monitor:
- per-pool GPU utilization, queued requests, average batch size
- 95/99th token latency, request success rate, kernel OOMs
- autoscaler actions: scale-up, scale-down, failed attempts
- infra errors: provisioning failures, terraform apply errors, state lock collisions
Alerting thresholds (examples):
- GPU OOM rate > 0.5% in 10m -> P1
- Queue length per GPU > 5 for 5m -> P2
- Terraform state lock collision -> P2 (investigate CI concurrency)

Team wiki & onboarding pointers
-----------------------------
- Quickstart: how to run the local terraform plan and test modules (link to repo README)
- Oncall checklist: what to look for during a capacity alert
- Ownership matrix: who owns each module/component and escalation contact

References and related docs
--------------------------

- gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026 (operational runbooks)
- infra-gpu-fleet-capacity-and-ci-cd-playbook-2026 (team playbook variants)

Appendix: quick checklist for changes
- Run `tf fmt` and `tf validate` locally
- Create PR with clear description and risk assessment
- Attach plan artifact to change ticket
- Ensure at least one recovery testing step post-apply
- Notify #infra-updates for any production capacity change
